Does central bank tone matter for Fama-French factor returns?

In October I presented our joint research with Bence Siket at the AFMLC 2025 conference at Corvinus University of Budapest. We asked whether the tone of central bank communication influences cross-sectional asset pricing, specifically the Fama-French factors.

Why tone matters

Since the 2008-2009 financial crisis, central bank communication, and speeches in particular, has become a crucial monetary policy tool. As Ben Bernanke put it: “Monetary policy is 98 percent talk and only two percent action.” Understanding how market participants perceive and respond to that talk matters for research and for investment practice alike.

Research question: Does the tone of Federal Reserve speeches have a predictive impact on the five Fama-French factors and the momentum factor?

Efficient markets or bounded rationality?

The question connects to an old debate. If markets are semi-strong efficient, public communication should not predict profitable factor returns, and only unexpected announcements should matter. Behavioural finance argues the opposite: investors process information imperfectly, and information may diffuse with a lag. Earlier studies find that the tone of ECB and Federal Reserve communication moves equity prices, volatility and trading volume, while others, such as Kurihara (2014) for the euro area, find no significant effect. Assessing the tone of speeches against factor returns is one way to test investors' bounded rationality.

Measuring tone

We compared several ways of scoring a speech as hawkish or dovish:

  • Loughran-McDonald (LM), the most widely used dictionary for financial text, which may lack explanatory power in a monetary policy context.
  • Bennani and Neuenkirch (BN), which sorts keywords into hawkish and dovish categories.
  • Apel-Grimaldi (ABG), which captures combinations of words, such as “inflation” next to “high” or “low”.
  • Our own dictionary, also built from word combinations.
  • An LLM, Gemma 3 through Ollama, prompted to score each statement on a hawkish-dovish scale and on how relevant it is to core monetary policy decisions, with a few worked examples in the prompt and the option to answer “None”.

The data

We scraped every speech by Federal Reserve officials from 2006 to the end of 2023 and identified the speaker. Between 41 and 95 speeches a year, and the share given by the Chair fell from about a third in the early years to under 10% in 2023.

What we found

First, the measures agree. The Apel-Grimaldi index closely mirrors the LLM scores, and both correlate with inflation and with changes in the Federal Funds rate, so they do capture the monetary policy stance. The LLM is marginally more consistent in deflationary periods, but the difference is small. The dictionary has a real advantage: it is transparent and reproducible, unlike an LLM black box.

Second, the factor returns. In bivariate regressions of each factor, in the same and in the next period, on tone, the picture across all speeches is weak: only a couple of dictionary-based results reach the 10% level. It changes when we keep only speeches by the Chair of the Federal Reserve. Then both the Apel-Grimaldi index and the LLM score are significant for all six factors, in the same and in the next period, while the Loughran-McDonald and Bennani-Neuenkirch dictionaries are not. The explanatory power is small in absolute terms, with an R² around 2%, but it is clearly there.

As speeches turn more hawkish, value stocks and conservative portfolios tend to outperform growth stocks and aggressive portfolios.

What it means

  • For investors: tone can be a useful input. A hawkish tone signals potential underperformance of momentum, growth and aggressive portfolios.
  • For policymakers: both intended and unintended effects of words in speeches can move asset prices, so careful and precise communication matters.
  • For academia: sentiment plays a meaningful role in asset pricing, which challenges the semi-strong form of market efficiency.

These are preliminary results. I want to thank Bence, who led several of the key empirical and modelling components with exceptional precision and dedication, and the organisers of AFMLC 2025 for a rigorous and intellectually generous environment. It is encouraging to see how fast AI-augmented financial econometrics is advancing.
